bib.title: A Categorical Archive of ChatGPT Failures

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Categorical Archive of ChatGPT Failures", Ali Borji (sole author; affiliation printed as "Quintic AI"). Preprint: the only venue marking on the PDF is "arXiv:2302.03494v8 [cs.CL] 3 Apr 2023"; the title page is dated "April 5, 2023".

COVERAGE: 41 of 41 pages, 82,370 of 82,370 chars. That covers the body (pp. 1-34), references (pp. 35-38, skimmed), Appendix A Math (pp. 39-40) and Appendix B Coding (p. 41). Figures 1-25 are screenshots, so their content was not extracted; I read captions only.

File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/borji-2023-categorical-archive-chatgpt-failures.pdf

CLAIMS

- claim: Failures are grouped into eleven categories, which the author calls arbitrary, non-exhaustive and overlapping.
  number: 11
  setup: Section headings 2.1-2.11, exactly as printed: Reasoning (sub-types: spatial, temporal, physical, psychological, commonsense); Logic; Math and Arithmetic; Factual Errors; Bias and Discrimination; Wit and Humor; Coding; Syntactic Structure, Spelling, and Grammar; Self Awareness; Ethics and Morality; Other Failures (an 8-item list: idioms, no emotional resonance, no distinctive perspective, verbosity, over-literal, neutral stance, formal tone, varied reaction to correction).
  quote: "these categories were selected arbitrarily and there could be more ways to categorize the failures ... It is possible for a single failure to be classified into various categories."
  where: p. 2

- claim: Examples are a convenience sample, mostly from Twitter and a community GitHub repository, plus some the author wrote; no counts or sampling method are given.
  number: none
  setup: The repository is Giuseppe Venuto's (named in the acknowledgement); the Marcus and Davis community error collection is cited as a parallel effort. Captions credit Ernest Davis, Tomer Ullman, Yann LeCun, Reddit and "formulated by me".
  quote: "Using examples mainly sourced from Twitter, the failures are categorized into eleven areas." / "I have been mainly inspired by this GitHub repository."
  where: p. 2

- claim: No failure rate is measured; the evidence is anecdotal throughout. The only attempt count is one coding task.
  number: 10 attempts, 0 correct
  setup: Centre-outward spiral matrix printing, a variant the author could not find online; the ChatGPT version is not stated.
  quote: "ChatGPT was unable to provide a correct response after ten attempts, five of which involved providing it with a sample input/output pair, while the remaining five attempts were made without any examples."
  where: p. 23

- claim: Re-testing on later versions was ad hoc. Two examples are reported as fixed in the Jan 30, 2023 version (the Winograd trophy/suitcase item and the race/gender "good scientist" prompt); there is no systematic re-run.
  number: none
  setup: Two single prompts, each tried once on the newer version.
  quote: "An older version of ChatGPT was unable to correctly answer ... but the latest version of ChatGPT (Jan 30, 2023) was able to generate the correct answer" (p. 3); "some of the failures may no longer exist in the newer versions of ChatGPT" (p. 2)
  where: pp. 2, 3, 11/14; the same caveat appears in footnote 9 (p. 19) and the Fig. 18 caption (p. 24)

- claim: Rewording a problem flips a correct answer to a wrong one, which the author reads as verbatim memorisation.
  number: 5 (correct) vs 8 (incorrect)
  setup: One prompt pair, single trials: "Mr. Smith has 4 daughters. Each of his daughters has a brother" against "My dad has 4 sons. Each of his sons has a sister".
  quote: "ChatGPT provided an incorrect response of 8. This highlights that ChatGPT can be prone to remembering things verbatim and can be quite rigid"
  where: p. 33

- claim: A perturbed known coding problem behaves the same way: the altered Advent of Code 2022 day 3 task was solved, but the sum-to-product variant failed twice.
  number: none
  setup: The author altered the wording "to reduce the probability of ChatGPT discovering it on the internet". The two wrong solutions are on p. 22 and in Appendix B.
  quote: "A subsequent attempt of posing the same question to ChatGPT resulted in another incorrect response."
  where: p. 22

- claim: Fair evaluation is blocked by contamination, and the author proposes private held-out test sets.
  number: none
  setup: Conclusion bullet; a proposal, not something built.
  quote: "I suggest constructing held-out test sets that are not publicly available, akin to how some image recognition competitions are administered."
  where: p. 34

- claim: Turning the archive into a benchmark is stated as an aim only; no dataset, scoring protocol or baseline is delivered.
  number: none
  setup: Introduction and the final conclusion bullet; the abstract links to a list of questions.
  quote: "the collection of failures outlined here can serve as a foundation for creating a comprehensive dataset of typical questions to assess future LLM and ChatGPT iterations, as well as generate simulated data for model training"
  where: p. 34; also "a standardized set of questions is necessary to track their progress over time instead of relying on subjective opinions" (p. 2)

- claim: Answers are inconsistent across repeats and sensitive to question order.
  number: answers "ranging from 2 to 4"
  setup: Repeated asks of one factual question, plus an order-swapped pair of joke requests.
  quote: "When asked the same question, its answers can vary."
  where: p. 33

LIMITS
- There are no rates, denominators, sample sizes, inter-rater checks or success cases, so the paper cannot say how common any failure is or rank the categories.
- Model versions are mostly unstated, and some Self Awareness examples are from Bing chat, not ChatGPT (Fig. 21).
- Examples are selected for failure, from public and viral sources that may since have entered training data. The author concedes fixes may already have landed.
- The taxonomy mixes capability failures (math, logic) with contested normative ones (humor, political stance, self-awareness), and the author concedes it is arbitrary.
- The "no world model" and memorisation explanations are asserted, not tested.
- Third-party numbers (630 political statements; 14 of 15 orientation tests) are secondhand.
- Dated: it covers ChatGPT from December 2022 to March 2023.
- The author concedes: "further systematic evaluation is required" and "I took a high-level approach" (pp. 33-34).

BUILDS ON
- Giuseppe Venuto's GitHub repository of ChatGPT failures (acknowledged, no year).
- Gary Marcus and Ernest Davis's community error collection (Substack, footnote 2).
- Azaria 2022 [3] and Frieder et al. 2023 [23], on math.
- Levesque, Davis and Morgenstern 2012 [38], the Winograd Schema.
- Guo et al. 2023 [24], the human versus ChatGPT comparison.
- Davis 2023 [19], the commonsense benchmarks survey.

CODE: Nothing worth keeping. The listings are ChatGPT outputs and the extraction letter-spaces them (pp. 21-23, 41).

FIGURES: One candidate, weak. Figure 5, p. 7: "Instances of ChatGPT's shortcomings in logical reasoning." It is a grid of six screenshot failures and shows what an archive entry looks like (prompt, wrong answer, source link). No figure shows the taxonomy or any data, so a table of the eleven categories built from the text would serve the note better.

PROBLEMS
- Hyperlinks ("here", "this GitHub repository") extract as bare words, so URLs for the question list and sources are not recoverable from the text.
- Figure content is images only.
- Code listings are letter-spaced and the Appendix A math is flattened (exponents and fractions lost).
- The paper has an internal cross-reference error: "Section 15" on p. 26 should point to the bias section or Fig. 15.
- There are no embedded instructions aimed at a reader or agent. Footnote 11, "Please try to run this code by yourself", is addressed to human readers and I ignored it.
- The author discloses that ChatGPT was used to edit parts of the paper.
